utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. I should like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the representatives from the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused in the courtroom. We have a witness today who is going to be testifying today and tomorrow. The Prosecution, according to it's schedule, has planned to hear the witness for three hours. Defence counsel will have three and a half hours according to our calculation, and for General Petkovic there will be one hour, and each of the accused will have 30 minutes each. So General Petkovic will have an hour, and the others will have 30 minutes, which means that if everyone sticks to the schedule, we should finish hearing the testimony of this witness tomorrow. I had asked the registrar to give me a breakdown of the time so far. By and large, the Prosecution has had for its examination-in-chief approximately 90 hours. The Defence teams -- Defence counsel and accused have had 125 hours, approximately 30 per cent more than the Prosecution. The Bench has had 23 hours for its questions, and to my great surprise, we have spent 80 hours dealing with procedural matters. Eighty hours to deal with objections and other things, which seems a very high figure. I think Mr. Karnavas is going to add to this because he wants to take the floor concerning a particular issue. This will be included in the proceedings. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. And I'm not trying to add to -- to this matter, but I'm glad the Court raised it, because we are concerned as well. The Prosecution, in fact it was Mr. Mundis who indicated that it was their belief that they would require their entire 400 hours allotted to them in order to present their case. We think that's fair, and we do think that they have been moving as expeditiously as they can, although there are the occasional hiccups which I'm sure we're going to face as well. If -- if we proceed in the following -- as we have in the past five months or so, it would appear that the Prosecution has approximately 15 more months before they can put on their entire case. That would mean their time, our time, the Court's time, and of course procedural matters. Obviously we can make some -- we should be making some adjustments on the procedural matters, but nonetheless, we, the Defence collectively, are quite concerned. We're concerned because the Registry, without consulting us at least, allocated 12 months and two weeks to the Defence as far as the Prosecution case goes, which means that if we go beyond that point, we run into financial problems. I don't want to get into that at this point in time. However, what I would like to do is bring this to the Court's attention and ask the Trial Chamber if it is possible for the Trial Chamber to give us a date certain when it believes the Prosecution must finish its case, whether it's the end of July or the beginning of October, but I think we're operating under hours, but it would be -- it would be enormously helpful to the Defence if we had a date. And why is that? Because then we, the Defence, would need to go and speak with the Registry. If it means the Defence would have to work four, five, six months without any additional resources, of course the Judges receive their pay every month plus benefits and what have you. The Prosecution the same. People that work in the booths and what have you. We cannot expect the Defence lawyers to be indigents and this may be somewhat of a trivial matter but we do have families. Behind every person there are tons of other people, loved ones that they have to take care of. So this is a realistic issue. All we're asking is perhaps the Court, you know, the Judges could meet and decide if it's possible to give us a date. I think it would be enormously helpful to the Prosecution as well if they knew more or less by which point in time they must finish their trial. That's it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you did well to raise this issue. On behalf of the Bench, I'm speaking in my own name, the other Judges can take the floor if they so wish. It is quite obvious that it's out of the question that you work without being paid. If the trial lasts through 15 months, and that would be the presentation case of the Prosecution, you would be paid for 15 months and not for 12 months. That would be totally unheard-of. Rest assured you will get the full support of the Bench on this. However, you have said that the Prosecution will have 15 months. I'm not quite convinced of this, because theoretically the Prosecution has to consider their witnesses. Some of them might be 92 bis or 92 ter or 89(F) witnesses. So I am sure that the Prosecution has room to manoeuvre here and can gain time. My concern runs as follows, and this is why I have mentioned it: I have realised that we spent 80 hours talking about procedural matters. So that is so much time which the Prosecution has not been able to use. Given the number of decisions we have taken, I think we shall certainly gain time on procedural matters. There will be fewer problems to contend with. And by gaining such time, the Prosecution will be able to present its case in the best manner possible. We have, however, spent 80 hours on procedural matters, which is huge. At this stage, Mr. Mundis, perhaps you don't have a clear view of the situation. The Defence team has told us that you still need 15 months for the presentation of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's entirely unclear precisely how long we will take. We've repeatedly indicated that we anticipate fully using our 400 hours. We have relied upon that figure in terms of our planning. We are doing everything possible to move forward as expeditiously as possible. Let me put this, though, on the record, that because we can't control the entirety of the amount of time used, the Prosecution does oppose the imposition of a date certain for us to complete the Prosecution case in chief. Our position is that looking at the numbers that the Registry has compiled for us at the direction of the Trial Chamber, our view is that having used approximately 90 hours to get through some 35 or so witnesses, we believe is an expeditious use of everyone's time, and we are continuing to endeavour to move as expeditiously as possible through use of all available Rules and jurisprudence of this Tribunal to meet that goal as quickly as possible. We certainly can understand the plight that the Defence are in. That's really a question between the Defence and the Registry and perhaps the Trial Chamber. What we would oppose would be any efforts to further reduce the scope of time that's available to us in order to solve the problem that the Defence faces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, but I won't be too long, I hope. I must say that I find it difficult to accept the attitude of the Prosecutor's office. I can understand that it is very difficult for you to foresee how much time you need because in fact you do not have full control. We don't, the Defence doesn't, no one has, but I think you could be expected and you must be expected to -- to make a considered guess, so to speak, a forecast on which the Defence can base itself in its legitimate quest for a regulation of its situation. We cannot leave it at that. It's not enough to say, "We don't know but we'll do our best." I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just briefly respond. Again, the problem that we face, and we've raised this issue repeatedly from the beginning, is the uncertainty as to how much time will be allotted for cross-examination. It's of course very difficult for us to factor in the amount of time that will be taken for questions from the Bench. If I were to tell you that we would require another 310 hours to complete our case or 300 -- roughly 300 hours to complete our case, that's fine if I assume that the Defence will get 300 hours of cross-examination, then that's 600 hours. That would mean that there would be in this factor no time for questions from the Bench, or we could arbitrarily say 10 per cent additional for questions from the Bench. I can tell you based on some statistical tracking that we've been doing that the Prosecution is taking a little bit less than one hour and 30 minutes per day, so that a full court day, whether it's 9.00 until 13.45 hours or 14.15 until 19.00, that's a full court day, we're getting in a little bit less than 90 minutes of Prosecution direct examination a day on average. That's what we've averaged thus far in terms of the number of witnesses and the amount of time that we've taken. I can guarantee you that we're working to solve this through the use of 92 ter, 92 bis, 89(F), moving as quickly as we possibly can. But at this rate, projecting out a number of days based on the number of witnesses we have left and the amount of time we have left is a highly arbitrary practice. I think, Your Honour, if -- with all due respect to everyone involved, the 90 hours that we've used thus far, we believe that we've been very expeditious in terms of moving and putting before Your Honours the evidence that you need in order to reach the decisions that fall within your responsibilities as a Trial Chamber here. We are of course open to further suggestions as to how to proceed, but it's extremely difficult for us to pick a date when we don't -- when we only control one -- approximately one-third of what happens in the courtroom in terms of cross-examination and/or questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not find this so difficult, if fact. You say now you have the experience that you use or that you can work one and a half hour per day. I am a bit less optimistic than our President about dramatic change and disappearing of procedural questions. I think it's inherent in these proceedings that they come up and it is the disagreeable task for the Defence, disagreeable for us, agreeable for the Defence to make things difficult. That's the rule of the game and we accept that. So you say you need another 300 hours roughly, 310. Two-thirds of it then -- if you have one and a half hour per day, working day here, that means you need a bit more than 200 days, and I think that would probably be a realistic estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Judge Trechsel. That's a very good point, and sitting four days a week, that's about 50 more weeks of straight sitting excluding any time off at Christmas -- factoring in, but 50 additional weeks including recesses probably means we need until the end of 2007 in order to get in our 300 plus hours that remain available to and which we've planned on using based on earlier Trial Chamber rulings. Now, again, if -- if the average number per day slips downwards, then we're into early 2008 before the Prosecution can finish its case. And again, I don't want to get boxed into anything, but it does appear to be the case, sitting four days a week whereby we're able to get in approximately 90 minutes per court day, we're taking about six hours per week for the Prosecution direct examinations. And yes, at that rate, it will be a little bit more than 50 weeks. So, yes, towards the end of 2007 at the rate we're going now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I share the point of view put forward by my colleague. The Prosecution needs to know where it's going, and you should really have a clear understanding of the presentation of your case. I have noted that as the number of hearings increases we will be able to gain time, because there is no need to repeat the same thing all over again and put the same questions, the question of water in Mostar and the question of the convoys. I think some questions have been addressed in great detail, and you needn't put that same question to every witness that's coming to testify here. However, and this is something that came to the surface last Thursday during the cross-examination, new -- new issue came to the forefront which was the issue of the exchange of prisoners. This is a theory put forward by the Defence, namely, the Muslims exchanged Croats in exchange for other Croats. So this should enable us to gain time. This was during the cross-examination, and I'm asking the Defence not to belabour the point and address the same issues all over again. These are things which the Bench is now familiar with. As far as procedural matters are concerned, I remember Mr. Murphy's objections last week. On several occasions we have heard objections to the effect that a document that was presented to the witness whereas the witness does not know the document, has not seen it, there is an objection. You know that the Chamber has already ruled on this even if the witness does not know the document but if the contents has something to do with the witness, then it can be admitted. There's no point in raising objections when these matters have already been dealt with. I'm fully convinced that we can only gain time by proceeding this way, and each and every one will be able to do this better and better. However, I don't know when the Prosecution will complete the presentation of its case given that the 400 hours that were allotted was a global figure. It is now for the Prosecution to give us -- to handle its witnesses according to their needs. To call four victims for the same fact is perhaps not necessary. Perhaps one victim for one particular fact is enough. It is perhaps not necessary to bring in the other three. So you may look into this. This is of course for the Prosecution to address these kind of issues. In addition, I have compared what we are doing with what other Chambers are doing, and so far our hearings have not been interrupted because witnesses could not be called to testify. I think our -- we've had no major drawback or hitch so far, and I think we have a good cruising speed. Nobody has been taken ill. So I think we can follow this pace in the future, and I think the Prosecution will be able to use up its 400 hours. So far having 90 hours, the Prosecution has had 25 per cent of its time, so you have 75 per cent left. But I do hope that out of the 75 per cent this might include a number of witnesses which you might not have to call to testify because others have testified on the same point. So you might wish to look into this again. We are going to hear an international witness today. If you bring the big boss, for instance, it is not necessary to bring the second-ranking person or the third-ranking person. It's for you to choose your witnesses properly so that we do gain time. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in connection with Your Honour's concerns about the time used for procedural matters, the 80 hours we've mentioned, I wish to remind the Chamber, now that we are analysing our use of time, that Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Murphy most often speak on behalf of all six Defence teams. In other words, I wish to point out that the Defence wishes to contribute to the saving of time, and as a rule, whenever we can, we appoint one counsel to deal with a certain kind of objection. I believe Your Honours have observed this. For example, I have always risen to my feet, for example, when there were discrepancies in the material provided and so on. But let me remind Your Honours that we are not a single Defence team. We are six Defence teams each with its own strategy and tactics, but we are all attempting to contribute to the economy of these proceedings and group together those objections we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I would just like to give you an example. You'd made a comment regarding a document which was mentioned the fact that somebody had died. The Chamber ruled on this. If this same matter occurs again, there's no need to bring it up because the Bench has ruled on this already. So if you say -- you stand up and you say it is a death certificate and there is something mentioned underneath it and I challenge it and we have already been faced with the same situation, then there is no need to stand up again. I think that is a good instance of where you might avoid standing up again because the Bench has stated its position on that matter so there is no reason why we should go back on our decision, particularly if it's been given in writing. This is just an example I wanted to give you. For instance, when a Defence counsel takes the floor, the Defence counsel usually takes the floor on behalf of the entire Defence team as far as procedural matters are concern. When Mr. Karnavas a while ago stood up, he stood up on behalf of the entire Defence team. It had to do, of course, with the fees to be paid to Defence team during the presentation of the Prosecution case. One of my colleagues to my right would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: It has already been quite a long one, but I would like to add the following: That so far the Defence spoke, the Prosecution spoke, and of course the Chamber spoke, but we have to really be aware of the fact that the -- as far as the timing is concerned, it is very important that we have to take into account the interests of the -- of the accused, because no doubt that -- that if we can finish with due attention to the accuseds' rights and to the basic Rule of this Bench and this Tribunal, then it would be indeed in the interest of the accused to have our case here to be finished in good time. Again, let me repeat with the best of the -- taking into account all of the relevant rules which have to be applied here. So that is why I would also add my voice to those who have asked for all the two parties to indeed observe the rules and to try to do their best, and even the Bench should take into account that very issue of the timing and probably having a bit less number of questions which we are doing, and at the same time the two other parties should take this into account as well. So that is what I would like to add to what has been said today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very briefly. In connection with the example Your Honour mentioned, you will recall that most of that discussion was carried on in writing. I raised an objection which I did have to raise only to reserve my rights and then dealt with it subsequently in a written motion precisely to save time. Secondly, Your Honours, we cannot know what facts we may have to refer to at the appeal stage should there be an appeal stage later on. The Appeals Chamber could say that we did not raise a certain objection during the trial, so we have to do this. And secondly, that we did not exert due diligence. Maybe that death certificate is a good example, although I might be able to see that Your Honours are inclined to accept it as an exhibit in spite of its deficiencies, which are quite evident, and Your Honours wish to leave it up to the weight to be attached to it, but for reasons of due diligence, I do have to object. Of course we can try not to do it in the courtroom. We can try to do it in written form, but at least the initial objection has to be in the courtroom. My learned friends and I, of course, have discussed this, and we are trying to use time as rationally as possible, and we often desist from raising issues which under normal circumstances, if we had enough time, we certainly would raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right. What I wanted to say is when you raise an issue at one particular time, then obviously it is a question of due diligence, but you should not raise the issue again a second time and a third time. I just wanted to clarify this. I've just asked the registrar to move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have the witness shown in straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon. While we're waiting for the witness, maybe I can just already inform the Trial Chamber that this witness will be a public witness and he will testify on the following counts: Counts 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 19, 20, 22 and 23. And his testimony will be relevant to paragraphs 64, 65, 66, 67 and 68 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bos, for telling us that useful piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I'd just like to check that you can understand what I'm saying in your own language, if your receiving the interpretation. If so, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm receiving the information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You're now going to testify. I'd like to ask you to stand and to answer some of my questions before you take the solemn declaration. Give me your name, surname and date of birth first, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Andrew David Williams and I was born on the 31st of May, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession or activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My current profession is a database loader for Stena Line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before a Tribunal, national or international, with respect to the events that took place in Yugoslavia or is this the first time you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the second trial I've attended, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for the transcript, which was the first trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Kordic/Blaskic trial, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a Prosecution or a Defence witness to the best of your recollection, or maybe a witness for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Prosecution witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As you are a Prosecution witness today. I'd now like to ask you to read the solemn declaration that Madam Usher is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just some information that I'd like to impart, but since you've already testified you'll know all about this. You'll first start off by answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. Mr. Bos will be asking the questions, and you probably met him this morning or yesterday. That is what we call the examination-in-chief, and the Prosecution has told me that they need approximately three hours for that. Of course, if it takes less time, the Chamber will appreciate that. Now, having completed that phase, the Defence teams, and as you can see there are a lot of Defence counsel, more than in the Kordic case, Kordic trial, anyway, the Defence counsel will be asking you questions after that, and I assume some of the accused who also have the right to ask questions pursuant to the Statute of this Tribunal. And the Chamber has decided set aside three and a half hours as Defence time. So if all proceeds according to schedule, you will have finished your testimony tomorrow. The four Judges sitting in front of you -- you just had three Judges in the Kordic trial, we are now four, and they can ask you questions at any time, and we shall certainly be doing so. Try to be as concise as possible in your answers, because as you know, your testimony is being coupled with documents there are going to be put to you as exhibits, and all this will be sized by the Chamber. So the Prosecution, I'm sure, will be showing you a whole dossier of documents, and you'll be asked to confirm the contents of certain documents. Having said that, I'm looking at the Prosecution, and I'd like to tell them that I have noted there are two documents of the -- of BritBat which are posterior to the departure of the witness, and I believe that the witness left his battalion in the month of May, whereas the documents are dated after that date. So, a priori, they are documents which the witness probably doesn't know. So he had direct knowledge of the previous documents prior to his departure, of course. However, having said that, without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few introductory questions. Is it correct that you joined the British army in May, 1976 -- 1967, I'm sorry -- 1976?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, although I understand your question, I don't hear any translation going on in the background. Yes, I did join in 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Are you having the English translation on your earphones?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that you served as an intelligence officer for the Cheshire Regiment from early November 1992 to early May 1993 at Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain what the role was of the Cheshire Regiment in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We had deployed as a battalion-sized group to Central Bosnia in support of United Nations operations. The battalion main base was in Vitez, and it had a company which I was part of. That was deployed into Gornji Vakuf as a sort of back-door company, so that should the main force need to leave the country quickly, we would hold the route open for them to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was that the only -- the only role of that battalion in Gornji Vakuf, or was there any other role?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We had two roles. We had our United Nations role, which was to support the distribution of aid and to support aid getting into the country, and we had a British army-type role whereby we located the headquarters of the various units, identified the commanders, identified where their heavy weapons were kept, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And approximately how many British soldiers were actually stationed in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was a reinforced company group of about 150 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Initially the commander was Major Alastair Rule, and he was replaced in March or April, 1993, by Major Alun Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, what was your specific role in the regiment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had two roles. My primary role for the mission that we were on, the aid mission, was to gain information on routes, checkpoints, and things like that, and to maintain a running brief so that convoys passing through would know that the route was open and that it was safe to go through. And I had a secondary role, a British army-type role, should the need arise, I would be the senior mortar-fire controller, artillery controller and airstrike controller.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just going back to that first role, did you do that on your own or did you have some colleagues with you who assisted you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: For more than half of the tour, I did that first role on my own, the information gathering, and I was reinforced in the latter part of the tour by a sergeant called Peter Dalton from the intelligence corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But did you have any assistance of persons who could actually speak the language?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Within the base we had two local interpreters, Belma and Alicia, and we also had a captain called Nick Short who spoke Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did this Captain Nick Short assist you on occasions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I liaised quite closely with both Captain Short, who also was a liaison officer, and also with another captain called Mike Hughes who was a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And both of them spoke B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. Only Captain Short actually spoke Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And in this role as -- as information gathering, did you draft reports?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I submitted a daily information summary to Vitez, which was then condensed into a battalion group information summary covering the whole battalion area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, we'll be seeing a couple of those documents later on, but let's just move on for now. So just briefly on your second -- you said you were a senior mortar controller. Is it fair to say that -- that with that specific function you would have good knowledge of weapons and weapon systems?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was what is classed in -- in the infantry as an alpha mortar-fire controller. Each infantry battalion has eight mortar-fire controllers and the alpha mortar-fire controller is the senior mortar-fire controller of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you arrived in the region in early November, 1992, what was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was largely peaceful. However, there'd been sporadic clashes just prior to and during our initial deployment between the armija and the HVO down in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to that, just more on the more overall situation before we get to the clashes between the HVO and the armija. What was the situation like in the region?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was largely static from a military point of view. The warring factions across most of the country seemed to have settled into static defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But who was fighting who at the time? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At that time there was a -- an alliance of sorts between the HVO and the armija against the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. And in that particular conflict the situation was static, as you just described?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Over most of the country it was static. Just prior to our deployment there'd been an advance up near Travnik by the Bosnian Serbs when the town of Jajce had fallen and the front line had shifted down to a small town called Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask you some questions on that. So you've just said that the town of Jajce actually had fallen. To whom had it fallen, and when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It had fallen either in late October or very early November, and it had -- it had been taken by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What kind of effect did this fall have -- had on the situation in the region?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was fairly chaotic. There was a large movement of refugees in that initial area and withdrawing forces from that area. It also impeded our commander's plans in that Vitez was all of a sudden within artillery range of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, maybe to assist the Court and -- and everyone else here in the court, we could maybe put a map on the ELMO which is Exhibit 9276, and as you can see, you have a bundle of exhibits there in front of you, and the usher is going to help you. On the bottom there are a couple of maps, and what I would like you to look at is exactly this map which is going to be shown to you now. This is map number 2 of Exhibit 9276, and it is in fact -- it depicts the municipalities of Bosnia. Maybe we can focus the map a little bit. It's still a bit out of focus. I don't know if we can focus it. Very well. Mr. Williams, could you just indicate first where is the municipality of Gornji Vakuf on this map.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's the municipality of Gornji Vakuf there at the point of the pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you've just spoken about the municipality of Jajce. Could you point at the municipality of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is the municipality of Jajce there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could you indicate on the map how the situation changed as far as front lines between the Serbs and the -- on the one side and the HVO and the armija on the other side after the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Within this immediate area, the front line shifted from somewhere in this region down to somewhere in this region, into the Travnik region.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why did all of a sudden Gornji Vakuf become an important region as a result of this fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The interior of Central Bosnia is very mountainous terrain, and there are very few good tarmac main roads in that area. As a result of the advance by the Serbs in that area, some of the roads became untenable and as a result the town of Gornji Vakuf became quite pivotal in that it was the only route from Split and Herzegovina, the western part of Herzegovina up into Central Bosnia. You had to pass through Gornji Vakuf and then up a track to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So if I understand your question correctly, as a result of the -- of the fall of Jajce to the Serbs, one of the routes into Central Bosnia was no longer accessible for the HVO and the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a main road that ran from Bugojno to Travnik, but it -- as a result of the fall of Jajce that became very, very close to the front line, and as a result it was not really suitable then for moving aid or indeed for our use.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. We'll leave the map there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I don't mean to interrupt, but perhaps -- I mean, the gentleman pointed to the map and of course we can read, but since we have someone here who was at the terrain at the time, perhaps he could mark the map and designate exactly where the lines were. That way we have something more concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, we can -- we can do so if that will help the Judges and the Defence. I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, Witness, maybe -- the usher will give you something to write on -- to write with, and could you just maybe first draw the front line as it was before the fall of Jajce and then, secondly, the front line after the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This will be very rough of where the line was. In that area it ran something like that as I recall. And then with the fall of Jajce, it shifted down to about that area there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And maybe you can mark the first line with a 1 which is the front line before the fall of Jajce, and the other line with a 2 as the line after the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned earlier that as a result of this -- of the fall of Jajce Muslims moved into -- moved out of Jajce into various municipality -- neighbouring municipalities. Did Muslims also move to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, some of them did move down to Gornji Vakuf and also into Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were also Muslim soldiers moving into Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the withdrawing armija unit moved into the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can you say something about the number of soldiers that actually moved into -- into the Gornji Vakuf area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The number of them that I saw were mainly living in the villages of Boljkovac and Voljevac which was just to the south of the actual town of Gornji Vakuf and they numbered approximately 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was the fact that both Muslim civilian refugees and Muslim soldiers that they were moving into Gornji Vakuf, was that a point of complaint by the HVO in the months of November and December?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was a source of some concern mainly due to aid and things like that, but at that particular point in time, it was not a major source of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did it became an issue after the conflict had started in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It became an issue just prior to the start of the conflict and then during the conflict itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you briefly touched upon Prozor as well, and could you explain to the Judges what was the situation in Prozor like when you arrived in the region. So November, December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There'd been some hostilities between the local HVO and the local Muslim population. They'd try to impose on the armija unit in that area that they must disband and become part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who is "they" when you refer to "they"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The HVO in Prozor. This had lead to some fighting within Prozor itself, and the imam was under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you visit the town of Prozor in that period?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. We actually -- on deployment we actually passed through the town, and there had been some fighting as we were in the process of passing through it. And there were some houses burnt and what not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah. So you answered my next question. What was the town of Prozor like when you -- when you visited it? How did it -- what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was tense. The streets were mainly empty. There were some freshly burnt houses that were still smouldering, and there were a couple of bodies that were lying on one of the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, according to your assessment, what kind of effect had the situation of the neighbouring village of -- municipalities of Prozor on Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The two communities within Gornji Vakuf became suspicious and distrustful of each -- or more suspicious and distrustful of each other than they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did activity of the HVO in Prozor in the latter part of 1992 raise some concerns for BritBat with regard to the situation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It raised a lot of concern, because we were concerned that if a major fallout occurred between the HVO and the armija in the Gornji Vakuf area, it would effectively cut the supply route into Central Bosnia, which would not only stop the aid moving into Central Bosnia, which was desperately needed as winter was just about to start, but it would also isolate the main part of our battalion group inside Central Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, in front of you you have two bundles of exhibits, and I would like you to look at Exhibit 922.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm at document 922 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you look at page 2 of this -- well, let me first -- no. Let me first look at page 1 of this report. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the battalion group military information summary that is generated -- was generated by the -- our battalion headquarters up in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Right. And in this particular report, you would have put your contribution as far as Gornji Vakuf was concerned?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, daily. As I said earlier, I would send a report up daily to Vitez, and then they would condense it and add it into this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, the document is a bit difficult to read, but it seems that it reads -- can you read what the date says?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It would appear to say the 1st of December on this document. However, in the Serbo-Croat version on the screen it says 17th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you look at page 2, it refers to tensions amongst Croat and Muslims, and it refers to tensions in Prozor. Is this actually what you were testifying about just -- just a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This would be part of the general increasing tension between the two armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you could read the last line, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It says -- I can't -- the first bit's blurred and then it says "Call-sign reported that two platoon strength HVO patrols," and then it gives two grid references, 1776, which refers to a one kilometre grid square -- no, sorry my mistake. It's blurred. Patrol. It's "patrols at" something. And then at grid Yankee Juliet 1369, which is a one kilometre grid square.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good idea to put right the mistake in the transcript straight away on page 17, line 19, reference is made to page 2 of the document and it says "Prozor". There's no mention of Prozor in page 2. It is Gornji Vakuf that is mentioned, and I think from previous statements by the witness this was mixed up. I think so that perhaps it would be a good idea to clarify is the document referring to Prozor or Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I can clarify straight away. If you would read the text under Gornji Vakuf, and then if you read the second and I will read it out. It says: "GV believed that if the HVO in Prozor continue in action, then conflict is inevitable." So there is a reference to Prozor although the heading says Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, GV, what would that abbreviation stand for?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The abbreviation GV stands for Gornji Vakuf. At this stage of our tour, anything that was reported by Gornji Vakuf, whether it occurred in Prozor or Tomislavgrad or whatever would appear under the heading Gornji Vakuf, which meant that the Gornji Vakuf office was the first office to deal with it. This particular report refers to Prozor HVO even though it is under the Gornji Vakuf title, because it was the Gornji Vakuf office that made the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Mr. Williams. Again coming back to that last line. Well, you've been referring to the grid reference, but -- so it talks about the presence of a two-platoon strength HVO patrols. Do you recall where these two platoon patrols -- where these were encountered?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Without a map to actually point to the specific grid square, I couldn't point it out. I put on here, but I can say that it is up around the village around the village of Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Which is in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's in the Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just to clarify, when it says two-platoon strength, how many men are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Two-platoon strength patrols would be approximately 25 to 30 men in each group. When they use the word "patrol," then that means that they were tactically deployed as opposed to just moving from one place to another. They were actually armed and were in tactical formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So if it was two patrols, we're talking about 60 men. And why was it worth reporting this in this particular report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At that particular moment in time, the HVO in Prozor were attempting to -- the villages up around -- including Here and around Here were Muslim villages and they tended to gravitate for trade and what not towards Gornji Vakuf. And the HVO in the area had blocked the roads with earth, dams, earthen constructions in attempt to force the people in that area to gravitate towards Prozor instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why do you think that they did this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was to try to bring them under Prozor's control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move back to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a follow-up question relating to the last sentence. You mentioned two HVO patrols. Why is there no mention of the unit whom these patrols belonged to? Because the HVO is a very general term here. Why does your report not specifically mention the unit in question? Unless it is something you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without actually speaking directly to patrols, it was sometimes very difficult to ascertain which unit they came from. A lot -- most of them did not wear the brigade flashes to identify their brigade, the brigade badge on their arm. However, the front line was nowhere near Prozor, and so if you saw troops in the Prozor municipality doing whatever soldiers do, it was fair to assume that they belonged to the Prozor HVO and not another HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The concern I have is as follows: Who were these units? Were these soldiers that belonged to a unit or were these members of the military police of the HVO moving around? When you see a patrol that include a handful of men, are these people wearing camouflage uniforms? Are these military police? Who are these men? This is a question I have. When you mention the point where you saw them GR 1369, that's an elevation point. That's a topographical data. But the observer, did the observer have a pair of binoculars? This is -- or a particular lens? Was this done visually. Was this done through drones? Was this provided through the intelligence services? How did you get hold of that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This information would have come from debriefing a patrol, one of our patrols that would have seen these two patrols. The grid 1369 refers to grid square 1369 on a map. So that's a one-kilometre grid square that the patrols were in. Other than the fact that they were HVO, there was no other information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one last because we could spend hours on this, just one last question. You talk about the HVO. Does this mean that you saw an insignia of the HVO on one of the men's clothing, or is it because these men were in possession of arms that you inferred that these were HVO men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO and the armija -- the armija tended to wear the Bosnian symbol on their sleeve, and if you saw a large group, most of them would have the Bosnian symbol on their sleeve. The HVO tended not to have flashes on their sleeves, and their type of combat trousers that they wore, the camouflage pattern on them was of a different design to the camouflage pattern that the armija wore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you describe to us in detail the camouflage uniform worn by an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the warring factions only wore the trousers. Very few actually had the jackets as well. And the type of camouflage uniform that the HVO tended to wear was of a darker pattern than the armija's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Darker. Does this mean black?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour. It's just a darker shade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see HVO members dressed all in black?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You do occasionally see -- we did occasionally see HVO soldiers or Bosnian Croat soldiers dressed in black, but not -- not all of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Moving back to Gornji Vakuf, Mr. Williams. How did the local HVO and ABiH troops react to the presence of UNPROFOR when you established a base in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The local HVO didn't really want us there, but the local Muslims did. They wanted us to see what -- what was going on, and they sort of looked on us as being something that would keep outside forces, outside influences under control by the fact that we were there. They wanted the outside world to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Why did the HVO not want you to be there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Specifically, I cannot answer that other than to say that they probably assumed that our presence there would impede what they were doing. And also, the -- they were suspicious of aims that we had or motives that we had for being there. They didn't like us nosing around and sticking our noses into things and asking their soldiers questions when we were on patrol and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On a local level, how did the Muslim and Croat troops get along with each other?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Initially to -- how we -- to what we saw, they were co-existing quite well, and our OC, our commander, helped them set up joint commissions to oversee police in a local -- I mean, local stuff like water and electricity and aid distribution and things like that, to help them work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What was the name of the local HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The local HVO commander was a gentleman by the name of Zrinko Tokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the name of the local HVO unit in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was the Ante Starcevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you describe Mr. Zrinko Tokic? What kind of man was he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He seemed to be a pleasant individual. He was never antagonistic or hostile towards us, although he knew where the line was and didn't -- at first didn't come too close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that in the -- in the course of, you know, near the end of 1992, that tensions increased in the region?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were some incidents that caused tensions to rise within the town itself towards the end of 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were some incidents. Could you explain what kind of incidents you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was an incident involving an HVO soldier who murdered a mentally retarded person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you give us more detail about this incident? What actually happened and when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Exactly when I cannot remember without referring to documents. He beheaded a mentally retarded Muslim and bowled the head into a Muslim bar like a bowling ball.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you refer to "he," who is he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Without referring to the documents, I cannot remember his name. However, when it was brought up later on in cease-fire negotiations and incidents that followed on the HVO did admit that he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: He was an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now if you could take the bundle of exhibits again and if you could look at Exhibit 759. Now, looking first at the first page again, this is again a Cheshire milinfosum as the ones you've been describing before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. When we first deployed we used to do them on these forms before we got computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This one is the 18th of November at 2120 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you could move to page 2, please. And I'm particularly interested in the last -- the bottom part of the second paragraph starting with "In Gornji Vakuf." Could you maybe please read this part going over on the -- on the third page?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: From the third line from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, starting, "In Gornji Vakuf tensions are reported to be high due to the HVO take over of a building belonging to the Bosnian army." Maybe continuing reading out.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "This was escalated when a Croat named Rajic Vlatko beheaded a local Muslim with a sheet of glass while drunk and possibly on drugs. The victim was reported to be paraplegic. The Muslims wanted Vlatko to go on trial in Zenica while the HVO said they would put him on trial in Mostar. The Muslims are now reported to have taken 10 Croats prisoner and tensions are still running high."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it says that the HVO were going to put this man on trial in Mostar. Was this person in fact taken to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The person was definitely removed from the area and almost certainly was taken to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe what the reaction was of Mr. Tokic, the local HVO commander on this incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, how -- did you -- when this incident happened, did -- did you or your commanding officer speak with Mr. Tokic about this incident and what was his reaction to this incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- when the incident happened, the soldiers from both communities immediately went to arms, and the situation became highly unstable. Our commander in Gornji Vakuf, Major Rule, got the two local commanders into the base and got the situation -- got them to sort the situation out, get the situation back under control and get their soldiers back to barracks and take the guns off the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did that work?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at Exhibit 778. Looking first at the second page of this document. Let me first ask you, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was shown it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you now look at the second page of the document. Who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is Zrinko Tokic, the head of the local Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you could briefly go through this document and -- and tell us if this is indeed the reaction that Tokic had to this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Both he and the local Muslim commander did not want to fight each other over this, and he was very cooperative in identifying the soldier concerned and that he would stand trial. The only sticking point of the whole thing was that the Muslims wanted him to stand trial in a normal court, and the HVO insisted that he had to be tried in Mostar. But other than that, they did agree that he should be arrested and should stand trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And this is -- this is it also reflected in the sentence and I'll just read it out on the first page where it says "Military prosecution will institute criminal proceedings against Vlatko Rajic and we strongly believe that the competent Mostar court will determine a just sentence it." Correct? This is in the middle of page 1.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, did this whole incident with Mr. Rajic ever came up again later on?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: When was hostilities of January and early February, 1993, started, during the cease-fire talks to try to stop that, this soldier was reported to be back in the Gornji Vakuf area fighting alongside other HVO soldiers against the armija, and it was continually brought up during the negotiations about why was this soldier here? Why was he not in prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how did the HVO respond to those questions as to why this soldier was here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They didn't deny that he was there, but other than that, they didn't go into detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how did the local commander, Mr. Tokic, react to this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was surprised that the soldier was back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was the -- any other incident that -- that increased tensions between the Muslims and the Croats in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was an incident with a school that was being used as a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you go into a bit more detail? When you say a school being used as barracks, by whom was this school used?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was initially used by both sides and then the HVO took it over completely, and that became a -- that caused some problems which were then exacerbated by the HVO holding a flag-raising ceremony during which a Muslim policeman was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Why was this Muslim -- why was this Muslim police officer shot at this flag-raising incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As they raised the Bosnian Croat flag, the policeman fired a shot over the top of it in protest and was himself in turn shot. It was a bit of a propaganda exercise by the HVO in that a TV crew from Croatian TV in Split had been brought up specifically to film the flag-raising ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this something abnormal for a media crew to come over for a flag-raising ceremony?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You would not expect a TV crew from a foreign country to come and watch the raising of a flag outside a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was this flag raising in fact later on broadcasted on Croat television?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We were informed that it had been shown on television and that it also had been used as propaganda and that the Croats had burnt their own flag but claimed that the Muslims had burnt it, which wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, again, did this increase tensions, this whole flag incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, again the tensions increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Tokic's reaction to this incident? Because I presume you sat around the table again with the local commanders to diffuse the tension?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Again, there was a meeting with the two local commanders and Major Rule, and again they managed to stop the situation spiraling out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this kind of meeting, did you attend this kind of meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These sort of meetings between the local commanders and Major Rule went on at the base every few days or so. Some meetings I attended. Most meetings I had some sort of little bit in, and some meetings I had no attendance in at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those cases where you did attend the meeting, what was your feeling about it? The local commanders who were there, did these people have a -- personally have room to manoeuvre, or did they always have to refer back to their superiors? What was your feeling about these meetings? I'm -- what I'm interested in is to know how much room to manoeuvre these local commanders had, or did they only adopt a position by referring to their superior command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially during the early part of our tour such as this particular moment in time, the local commanders used to sort it out between themselves with the assistance of Major Rule. They were -- both of the local commanders knew each other and tried whenever their soldiers were starting to become a problem, they did actually try to stop it. Very rarely did they have to -- at this stage, did they ever ask a higher level or were constrained by a higher level in what at the did or said. However, as I'm sure the Prosecutor will show later, that changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are speculating now on what the Prosecution is going to demonstrate. Let me give you an example of something you're very familiar with. This Muslim mentally retarded person who was beheaded, this was a very serious case. The local commander with who you must have certainly discussed this incident, this local commander, was he able to handle the situation on his own, or was it something that was totally out of his control and that he had to refer back to the superior command? I want to know what degree of autonomy these local commanders had vis-a-vis their superiors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The diffusing of the situation and the removal of their troops back to barracks would have been done at the local level. As to exactly where the soldier would go to stand trial, there would be input from higher authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the law that governs an army, when a military person commits a crime of this kind, this person will be tried by a military court, and when there is a conflict, can the local commander not set up this military tribunal? Why did this person have to be sent to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His -- his presence in the town was making the situation worse, so he had to be removed from the town. The Muslims wanted him to go to Zenica to stand trial, and the HVO would only accept Mostar. But he had to leave the town because his presence there was making the situation worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having specified this. It will now be time to have our technical break. It is now 20 to 4.00, and we shall resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, could you look at Exhibit 1068. We left off talking about the flag incident, and I just want you to -- you have that exhibit in front of you, 1068?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's a difficult to read. If you look at the front page -- but if you see what the date of this report is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can just make out that it is sometime in January, 1992. It may be the 6th, I think. I'm not sure because it's blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go for 6th January. If you look at the third paragraph on the first page. Is -- does that describe the incident that you just testified before the break?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that describes the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, from that day onwards, so we're talking about 6th of January, 1993, what happened in the days following this flag incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a noticeable fracture between the commands of the local HVO and the local armija. Although the situation diffused slightly, it never diffused back to the level it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And in your optic -- so you said hostilities increased. In your optic, who was the main instigator in these hostilities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In my opinion it was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If you could look at Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. The third paragraph of the document that you have in front of you, it says that the commanders could calm the situation down and most of the -- were able to calm the situation down and that most of the soldiers returned back to barracks. Now, in Gornji Vakuf, the HVO, were their barracks there? Did the HVO have barracks there in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they did, their main barracks in Gornji Vakuf. Their main headquarters was in a factory complex right next to where we were, and they had soldiers billeted in various buildings around the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the ABiH, where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their -- Your Honour, their headquarters was in the town, and then they had soldiers billeted around the town, many of whom were married and lived in their homes with their families. The same as the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The married people, they would go back home every night, and those who weren't married stayed on in the barracks? How did that function? Is that how it worked? Is that how the local commander had things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By and large, Your Honour, that's how it operated. They were locally-raised brigades, and when -- they seemed to be through a cycle of some of them being on the front line, some of them being prepared ready to rotate through the front line and some who stood down on a lower level with their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me that explanation, because it's a subject that was raised several times previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at Exhibit 1094. Looking at the first page of the document, Witness, this is again a Cheshire milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is from the 11th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to focus your attention on the last page of this report, which is page number 4. And could you please read out what has been written on this page.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On page 4 is a comment on the report on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It says: "The situation in Gornji Vakuf has been extremely tense for some time now, and it was believed inevitable that conflicts would start sooner or later. Novi Travnik is still extremely tense and the chances of a conflict between the Croats and the Muslims there is very high. This could again spill over to Vitez as well, as stated in milinfosum," that's military information summary, "number 71 dated the 10th of January, 1993. The situation is not helped by the arrival of HVO soldiers from Herzegovina who seem intent on antagonising the situation and starting trouble. Comment ends."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you have drafted this comment in this particular report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The actual report itself that the comment is made on I wrote. The comment is a general comment that -- linking the report -- the two last reports on the previous page and giving an overall interpretation of what it could mean and what could happen if it wasn't brought under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, in that last sentence it talks about the arrival of HVO soldiers from Herzegovina, and this is a report on the 11th of January. What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This actually refers to Travnik and Novi Travnik, and it actually refers to a unit called the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And -- so you say it talks about -- it talks about the unit arriving in Novi Travnik, but how would this happen -- have an effect on what's happening in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- both -- the soldiers in both local forces were very susceptible and suspicious of what went on around them and in areas that bordered on their areas. So if one area destabilised, unless it was brought under control quickly, it would destabilise the next area. So that particular unit arriving in Novi Travnik and the trouble associated with it would then destabilise Gornji Vakuf as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to get things clear here, and it's important with relation to the situation in Gornji Vakuf. The commentary, you mentioned several incidents, the flag incident, then the decapitation of the Muslim handicapped person, et cetera. Now, this could have given rise to greater tension, but there could have been more political reasons for that too. The transfer to Gornji Vakuf, other exterior elements might have had a hand. Now you seem to go along that line, because you say with the arrival of soldiers from Herzegovina that the situation was aggravated. So as far as you were concerned -- you have a privileged observer because you were in situ. Now, this rise in tension, was it due to local reasons purely or for reasons from outside with this situation being created outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were several factors that were not helping the situation. One was the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, which was slowly but surely being leaked into the media and becoming public knowledge, and part of that peace plan was the cantonisation of Bosnia, which included Gornji Vakuf being handed over to the Bosnian Croats. In addition, there was within the Bosnian Croat community a desire to form a state called Herceg-Bosna, which again was also starting to manifest itself in that they were issuing number plates for cars and things like that. And so the Muslim community in that area felt very threatened by all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: In military terms, how did you analyse the arrival of the soldiers from Herzegovina? Was there a military necessity for reinforcement by local units? Why did these soldiers from Herzegovina suddenly appear on the scene? What would your comment be about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the specific reason why that particular unit appeared on the scene, but that particular unit was associated with trouble. They would destabilise an area very quickly by their presence. So whenever it showed up, we became more aware of what was going on around us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, this unit, did it depend on a chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this particular stage we were in the very early weeks of our deployment. We'd been there approximately about -- by this stage about two months. The -- it appeared to us that the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade were -- were a commander's reserve. They didn't actually belong to a specific operation zone. They came under the direct control of the headquarters in Mostar and were sent to specific areas for specific operations, either to reinforce a front line if it was under pressure, or to exploit an advance if they'd made an advance, or just to generally bolster up that area for a particular reason. An operational manoeuvre group of sorts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English you said a "specific operations." That's the term you used. Now, is that how we should understand this, or should we understand it as being for special missions as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour. They were a unit that the HVO had who they could quickly put into an area and quickly change the balance of power within that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it an elite unit in a way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was above the normal HVO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you -- as we are at this, can you indicate the size of the unit more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You -- yes, Your Honour. You very rarely saw an entire brigade in one -- in one chunk, in fact. I don't recall ever seeing an entire brigade. Most of these brigades were not of the same size as a British army brigade. You would see -- ordinarily when you saw the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade you would see anything from a company to a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The questions of Your Honours have moved me a bit up in my outline. Some of those questions were on the next page of my outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But just to come back to a couple of answers that you gave in response to Judge Antonetti's questions about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. You've said that the things happening on the ground were also related to what was happening with the negotiations on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Could you elaborate a little bit on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've tried not to intervene unnecessarily, but I've observed that Mr. Bos has not tried to elicit from this witness what his qualifications are to comment on political or other events that were going on on the ground and the source of his information. I think we may have arrived at the point where that would be desirable if we're going to get into specialised things like the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Perhaps he could explain how the witness is qualified to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. You broached the Vance-Owen Plan. I didn't mention it when I asked my question. Now, did you have any particular competence or authorisation in Gornji Vakuf which would inform you about developments in Geneva and what was going to be put forward within the Vance-Owen Plan? Did you have information about that? Were you briefed about that in any way? Were you placed in a position where you would be briefed, or was it rumour going around among officers? Did you speak about it or did your unit, BritBat -- was your unit BritBat very well-informed about diplomatic developments in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- yes, Your Honour. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan at this stage was becoming public knowledge and was appearing in local newspapers. We used to as well produce a map of Bosnia for various things, and one of the maps that was -- we had a map of the front lines, for instance, and a map that detailed where different headquarters are, and we also had a map that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] BritBat, your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.
