utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "us", do you mean BritBat, your country? The battalion or your country, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour. As I recall the maps were made by the royal engineers mapping section on behalf of the UN. There was a series of maps based on the outline of Bosnia and one map would have the front line and another map would have different things on. We had one map that showed where the cantons had been proposed. And at this stage it also started appearing in the newspapers which were flown out to us from the UK and we also had regular briefings as part of our orders process, which not only was about the situation in Bosnia, but was also about the political situation behind the scenes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, I think that answer satisfies you, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Partly, Your Honour, yes. I was also interested in the witness's personal qualifications to comment on these things, but I can get into that in cross-examination if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a British officer, did you have any special qualifications in order to be able to understand what -- how plan could contribute to the situation and how the negotiations in Geneva could contribute with respect to the problem of cantonisation, population displacement, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was part of the military intelligence set-up in that -- in Bosnia, and my specific area was Gornji Vakuf. I was -- I received regular briefings and also handed information up the chain of command as well as down. I used to on a regular basis speak to people via interpreters and to gauge their feelings about things. It was -- once the outline of the cantons became public knowledge, the Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf were adamant that even if President Izetbegovic signed it, they would not hand Gornji Vakuf over to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they tell you or was this a conclusion drawn? Was it the commander of the ABiH who told you that, or was it a synthesis that you made of the general mood and atmosphere that prevailed locally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a little bit of all of that, Your Honour. The command structure of the -- the town were not happy with the cantonisation. The locals themselves were opposed to it, and it was -- it was a general mood throughout the Muslim population of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic. You've been on your feet several times now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we'll save a minute or two. The witness made mention of going to the front line twice, the front lines he said, when he spoke about the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade and in response to your own question about the maps. Perhaps it would be a good idea, because I know from previous witness testimony, that quite obviously he means the separation lines between the army of Republika Srpska and the HVO and ABiH together on one side. So could we just verify that? Otherwise, we're going to have to lose time during the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you be more precise, because a moment ago when you showed us the map and you mentioned a front line, I was going to ask you who was behind that front line. So for the record, could you be more specific? The front line, it was facing Republika Srpska or was there a second front line between the ABiH and HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this stage when -- when I refer to the front line, I mean the front line between the Bosnian Serb army and the HVO and the armija Bosnia on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understood it as well, but you've explained it properly now. Mr. Bos, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just -- just one other question on -- on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. You've stated -- you've spoken about the reaction of the local Muslims to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. What was the reaction of the local HVO and the HVO in general to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, I butted in too soon. They were supportive of it. They saw it as a good thing locally. They were -- but then they were going to be given control of that canton, so they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you please look at Exhibit 1087. Have you seen this document before, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was shown it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is Serb brigadier Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He's Chief of Staff of the HVO and he was based in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Very vaguely, once or twice, but not a face-to-face introduction or anything like that. I was present at places where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What's the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is the 9th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was this order about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This -- this -- in the British army this would be a stand-to order. Basically it's an instruction to all operations zones that in view of the forthcoming talks in Geneva, he's ordering them to step up their combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when there is reference here "In view to the forthcoming talks of Geneva," what is this order referring to here now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He's talking about the -- when he mentioned forthcoming talks in Geneva, he's referring to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question leads to another. The Prosecution has presented you with an order where we can see that General Petkovic is asking for three men to be placed in a high position in military terms. Now, BritBat, did you have a liaison officer with the HVO to liaise with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We had liaison officers all over the country who liaised with local commanders on both sides and in the areas where they could also with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who was your liaison officer vis-a-vis the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in Gornji Vakuf our -- our liaison officer at this stage was Captain Mike Hughes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, an order of that level, because it came from Mostar from General Petkovic himself, would your liaison officer know the existence of an order of this kind even if it was confidential, but would this type of document come to the ears of a liaison officer who was doing his work in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost certainly not, Your Honour. This would be a highly confidential document within the HVO. Like it says on the document, "Military secret."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But when an army is reinforcing, there's signs, are there not? If an observer is there, an intelligence officer, would there be grounds for you to conclude that something was afoot, something was happening? So in situ in Gornji Vakuf, did you observe a note as of the 9th of January, 1993, a sort of mobilisation or HVO reinforcement either because they were calling in reservists or because they were not granting any more permission to leave or logistical elements arriving? I don't want to go into military technology, but did you yourself note that something was afoot, that something was being prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew from the previous incidents the reaction from the local forces to that, that the situation between the two allies or nominal allies was highly unstable. With the constant -- within Gornji Vakuf, with them constantly going to arms with each other, it would have been very difficult to notice that this document was causing a reinforcement. Any reinforcements that were going on we would have assumed was because of local problems. As for the logistics and the movement of troops and lorries with ammunition and such like, the main route into Central Bosnia, as I said earlier, was through Gornji Vakuf, and it was -- there was a constant flow of traffic back and to, so you would not necessarily have noticed that they were actually reinforcing to do anything. The -- for instance, the presence of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade that we were talking about earlier may well be linked to this document, but without a direct link you can't actually say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On page 44 of the transcript, which is about 10 minutes ago, I suppose, on line 23, 24, when -- when you were posed the question by the Presiding Judge about the political reasons why the HVO would have started non-military operation in Gornji Vakuf, you said that there was a desire to form a state called Herceg-Bosna. Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, was -- was this political desire to form this -- this state, was this something which was initiated from the local government, or was this initiated from a more --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, how can the witness possibly answer that question? I object. I object to that. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you should have asked him before that whether he was qualified in any way to understand political issues, local political issues, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did you know anything about the local HVO politicians operating in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Very little. I tended to concentrate more on the military side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you said that -- when you just said on page 44 that -- that there was a desire to form a state called Herceg-Bosna, what made you say this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were complaints from the Muslim population to our commander that the HVO were making them change number plates, not specifically in our area, more from Prozor and the areas beyond that, to a number plate with a Herceg-Bosna shield on as opposed to the armija -- sorry, as opposed to the shield of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that they were also demanding that when they passed through certain checkpoints that they had a visa to do so, which could actually only be obtained from the HVO office, which in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at Exhibit 1184. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. Well, I saw it yesterday, but before then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just -- could you maybe look at page 2 and tell us what is the date of this document.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The document is dated the 18th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And moving back to page number 1, who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Dr. Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Prlic was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Other than he was a politician, I'm afraid I don't know at what level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document, would that confirm your statement that there -- that political influence from Prozor and outside the area were -- were relevant as to this -- as to your statement that the desire to form a state called Herceg-Bosna was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour, this time. I've been very patient today, and I've been holding back my fire, but this -- this goes beyond the pale. How can you draw that sort of conclusion, not to mention that it is also leading. I mean, if I could give my friend a suggestion, it might be that he could show the document and say, "What from the document can you derive?" You know, but then to lead and suggest what the answer should be so the gentleman can just say, "Well, yes, I guess so. I don't know." He doesn't have the foundation. The gentleman does not have the proper knowledge to answer that question. It's leading, and I believe that the witness has been poisoned to the extent with the leading nature of the question that he can no longer give us an objective answer at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, try to address this issue in a less questionable way if you find this document of any interest to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read the document and tell us what you would conclude from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this question is even less proper. The witnesses aren't here to make conclusions unless we're dealing with expert witnesses, but to tell us the facts, to address the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have a document here that comes from the president of the HVO and which is addressed to Gornji Vakuf, i.e., to the military authority there, to the municipal authorities, but also to the population at large. I read here that the population must be informed about what this document contains. You also said that you were in contact with the people there. According to what you know, around the date at which this document was prepared, around the 19th or the 20th of January, did the people in Gornji Vakuf get to know about this document? If that was the case, was it something that you were informed about? And the second part of my question is this: Does this document and what it contains tell you with what you knew was happening on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Firstly, I don't know whether the Croat community in Gornji Vakuf were told the contents of this document, and it was nothing I was -- as a result, I was not informed about it. The document itself reinforces the general mood of what was going on on the ground at the time. Basically saying if you -- that the -- the HVO would protect the Croat community in that area, and if need be, they would reinforce it from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Williams. Let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess I don't want to move on at this point since the gentleman did bring it out. There is something to the extent -- it says here about being left to the mercy of the Muslim extremists. Perhaps the gentleman might be able to assist us. Were there any Muslim extremists such as the Mujahedin in the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This is subject for cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw this sentence also and I was tempted to ask you that question, but given our time constraints I refrained from it. Yes, Mr. Karnavas would like some clarification about this. This document clearly states and clearly talks about Muslim extremists. What does this mean? Why are Muslim extremists mentioned here? The Defence counsel would like to know whether these Muslim extremists weren't in fact Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. In our particular area, there were no Mujahedin. There were -- there was an extremist brigade in the Muslim army. As I recall, it was the 7th Muslim Brigade, but that was not deployed in our area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that the 7th Muslim Brigade was extremist. Why was that the case? According to what criteria do you say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It carried with it a number of external Muslim fighters that had come from other Muslim countries. The Muslim army itself, the armija, had problems with that particular brigade themselves. Bosnian Muslims are European. They're not like Muslims from other -- from some of the more extreme Islamic states which is where some of these fighters had come from, and they were a constant thorn in the side of the actual armija itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We now can move to a separate topic, a new topic, which is the military -- the strategic military reasons for the HVO to attack Gornji Vakuf, and for that I would like you to look at one of the maps which is map number 24 in the bundle which is on the overhead projector. And maybe again, if you wish, you could mark the map, but could you briefly explain what the HVO was trying to achieve from a strategic military point of view when they started the attack on Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I have to object. I don't mean to disrupt, but if we could lay a foundation as to this particular question, because it assumes, first, that the gentleman knows what the HVO's intentions were. Now, he can give us a foundation as to the strategic importance of the area, which obviously would cut both ways, both for the Muslims and for the Croats, and then he can proceed from thereon step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness monitored the situation on a daily basis during the conflict, and I think he is able to talk about these matters. And if the Defence wishes, so we can first start on a more general point of view asking -- putting the question as to why Gornji Vakuf municipality was an important municipality, but I think he can also talk about more -- in more detail as regards to what the HVO was trying to achieve in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In military terms, in what way was Gornji Vakuf and its surroundings of strategic importance for the HVO? What was at stake here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The actual town itself sat -- sat astride the only supply routes up into Central Bosnia from this -- from the southern part of Croatia and from Herzegovina. The main road running into the country through Tomislavgrad on to Prozor was under HVO control. From Prozor up towards -- up to the Makljen checkpoint which was a checkpoint on top of a hill between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor was under HVO control. The town of Gornji Vakuf and the road junction where the track went up into Central Bosnia and the road went up into Bugojno was open to -- open to being closed by whoever controlled the town of Gornji Vakuf. If you controlled Gornji Vakuf, you controlled access to the whole of that part of Bosnia. If it was the armija that controlled Gornji Vakuf, they could cut the aid going into the Croat community. They could stop the HVO in Central Bosnia from being reinforced or resupplied. If the HVO controlled it, they could do likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about two routes that were important. Would you maybe be able to make a drawing of those two routes that went through Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first route was a proper main road that went from Gornji Vakuf. It went from Gornji Vakuf up to the town of Bugojno, and this was a proper road, tarmacked, two lanes. The second --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but would you continue that route passing Gornji Vakuf going to the south?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It went down to Prozor, through the Makljen checkpoint, which is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. That will be sufficient. And then this -- this second route?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The second route was a bulldozed track that went through the hills and the local name for it was the "Road to Salvation" and it went off in that general direction up into Central Bosnia to Vitez and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who controlled this second route?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Nobody actual little controlled it as such because it passed through both Croat and Muslim areas, and there were both HVO and armija checkpoints on that route. But if you controlled Gornji Vakuf, then you could control that route because quite simply you could close it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that because of the road situation the HVO felt that this entire area was of strategic importance to them, and that would justify that. Would there be any other reasons? Would there be any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was explained to me once by an HVO officer, Your Honour. I can't recall which HVO officer it was, but they had name. You would have to look at a bigger map of Bosnia. In the centre of Bosnia were the Croat communities Vitez, Busovaca, places like that. Surrounding them were Muslim communities such as Zenica and whatever. They called -- that particular officer referred to that as the Belt of Islam, and they needed to punch a route through the Belt of Islam and link up all the Croat communities in one continuous chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you look at the map, the one you've got before you, you can see there are some red dots and some green dots on there. In green are the Muslim community. The red dots represent the Croat communities. An observer could easily see that in the Muslim communities. In the mostly Muslim communities, we have a lot of Croat communities. Was this something which could have been considered when preparing a military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You would need to address that situation particularly for the security of your own rear areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that given a -- the people living in these communities, the -- you had to exert control over those communities which were not majority communities, so to speak. The HVO had no interest in controlling those communities which are in green on the map, namely Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular moment in time, Your Honour, no, because the route was open. But the situation deteriorated rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another aspect which you do not talk about: Now, the ABiH army, as far as the breakdown of the army was concerned, the BiH was in the same situation as the HVO? They were short on numbers also? How did you analyse the situation at the time in terms of military strength on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Both -- when they referred to a brigade, it was not as big as a British army brigade. It would be about the size of a reinforced battle group in British army parlance. Both sides were underequipped. However, the armija was more underequipped than the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the ABiH was in a position of inferiority in strictly military terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Locally, numerically, they were about evenly matched, but the HVO had more access to heavy weaponry than the armija did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please proceed. We might get back to this issue later on in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just -- Witness, maybe could you have a look at Exhibit 1104. Looking at the front page, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Again, this is the battalion military information summary. It's a bit hard to see in the English version, but it's from the 12th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you please move to page 2, and I would like you to refer to the top paragraph, and could you please read out the -- what is it, in line seven where it starts with "Comment."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "The HVO appear to have effectively sealed the north and south routes out of Gornji Vakuf. The only route which is now accessible to the BiH," that's the armija, "is the route north-east to Novi Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, going back again to the map on the ELMO, and this is the 12th of January, can you explain what the HVO was trying to do around that time when it says here that they were effectively sealing off the north and the south routes? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: By sealing the southern route, you guarantee your own rear security, and by sealing the northern route you prevent reinforcements coming from Muslim units or armija units up in Bugojno, Novi Travnik, Travnik area from coming down into the Gornji Vakuf area. Although you wouldn't be able to stop them coming through on foot, you would be able to stop any big movements by vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could you next look at Exhibit 1209, please. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was shown it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is dated the 19th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's commander Zeljko Siljeg, who is the commander of OPs on North-west Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know commander Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not personally, but, yes, I do know him. I've met him several times. More than several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We'll get back to that. Just on the point we're discussing right now, if you look at the start of the reports, the first -- read the six -- the first six lines.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "As we informed you today in an interim report, we have moved on to offensive operations. Some key facilities south of the town of Gornji Vakuf were taken: Mackovac Brdo, the relay. So that the towns were almost encircled. So to each village in -- Buvnjaci village, settlement were also taken. We have unintelligible village which is in tomorrow's plan surrounded; Gornji Hrasnica is taken, Duratbegov and Drazov Dolac are surrounded. There are destructive operations in other villages."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay, you can stop there. It talks about a number of villages and let me first say, between brackets it says, the Mackovac Brdo and the relay. Now, do you know what's been referred to as the "relay"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, the relay is a hill that looks over Gornji Vakuf on the south-west corner, about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you maybe mark that with your pencil and maybe put an R there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Marks] It's a very prominent hill. It's called the relay because it has a disused big radio mast on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What is the importance of the hill?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf is in a valley. The hill is quite large and overlooks most of the town. If you were on top of the hill, it -- with direct fire weapons it's very easy to dominate the southern half of the town completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it talks here about a couple of villages here in this report as well. It talks about Zdrimci, Gornja Hrasnica and in fact in the fourth line where it says "illegible village". Could you please have a look at the B/C/S version of this document and look at line four. Are you able to read what is -- what is missed by the -- by the translator? It's on line 4, the last word?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Salodrica [phoen], something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, these villages that I refer to here, so this is Zdrimci and this is Uzricje and Hrasnica. Can you locate those villages here on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Zdrimci is this village here. Hrasnica is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: They've become unreadable since you've marked -- made other markings. Okay. Thank you. Now, what would be the importance for the HVO to take control over these villages?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They overlooked the roads, and so even though they -- the HVO may control the road, it would still be able for the armija to fire down onto the roads. So if you wanted to secure the road properly, you would need to secure an area each side of the road to -- at least as far out as small-arms fire to prevent interdiction on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move again to a different topic again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you address another topic, I'd like to talk about this document again. This report which follows on an interim report is -- is addressed to Siljeg who must be on the ground. I realise that he sends this to the HVO, to the Operational Zone, north-west Operational Zone, but I also see that a forward command post is mentioned here also. According to what you know, was there a forward command post, an IKM, which controlled the entire military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was a forward command post, what we call a Tac HQ which was located in a village called Pidris, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how did you know that? How did you know that there was this forward command post there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The actual reason how we knew it was there I can't remember, but that's where it was and we used to collect Colonel Siljeg from near there when we used to take him down to his cease-fire talks. Also, as I recall, it came -- the information that it was actually at Pidris came from the armija, who had debriefed locals who had been moved out of that area. However, I can't -- I can't hand and heart say specifically that's where the information came from, but that's where his Tac HQ was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, around the time that the hostilities had broken out, did you recall attending a meeting where the HVO issued some sort of ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were cease-fire negotiations on virtually an ongoing basis where cease-fires were promised and within minutes it broke down or never came into effect at all. The longer this particular conflict went on, the higher up the people who attended these cease-fire conflicts seemed to be. The particular one, I think, to which you're referring, it was a delegation from Mostar, and also present was I believe Colonel Merdan and -- from the armija and also a major from Zenica, his security officer, Selmo Cikotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll just interrupt you there. When you say a delegation from Mostar, who does this delegation represent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were three or four people from Mostar, I think, one of which was a gentleman called Colonel Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But who were they representing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were representing the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you said there was a gentleman called Colonel Andric. Was there anybody else from this group of four that you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I -- I cannot specifically recall any of the names of the others or exactly how many of them there were. Colonel Siljeg may have been there, but I can't recall. There were that many meetings that were going on to try to stop this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When did this meeting start?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It started in -- as I recall, it started probably either just before or just after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What was the topic at the meeting? What was the -- why was --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was to try to defuse the situation and to get external soldiers from both sides removed from the area. At this stage, our aid convoys had stopped up into Central Bosnia, and our prime concern was to get that route back open and get the aid back into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't specifically recall it other than it is -- it was in January. Possibly after the middle of January, but I can't be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just spoken about a convoy stopped in Central Bosnia. Where was it stopped? What locality was that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of the convoys had stopped, Your Honour. There were no aid convoys going in and none coming out. They were -- as Gornji Vakuf was the only way in and out, the lot had stopped, so there was to aid being delivered into Central Bosnia and no empty aid lorries coming out to be reloaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you explain what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The meeting dragged on for most of the day. I wasn't present through all of the meeting, but it dragged on through most of the day. Basically, the HVO was stalling and stalling and being more belligerent. At the -- the meeting was ended by the HVO when Colonel Andric read out an ultimatum informing the Colonel Merdan from the armija and all the other people that were at the meeting that unless the Muslims disarmed they had two brigades ready to attack the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the other participants at the meeting on reading out of this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Everybody was a bit shocked, because although the situation was bad and there were exchanges of gunfire and the HVO had cut the town off, nobody expected them to decide that they were going to attack the town properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how did the outcome of this meeting affect the situation on the ground in Gornji Vakuf in the following days?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- the meeting broke up there on the spot because there was not a lot more that could be said. Colonel Merdan from the armija was very upset. He actually thought that they would lose the town. He didn't think his own men would be able to hold it. Our concern was how long would the fighting go on, because we needed to get the aid moving again because it was winter. And also, the safety of the civilian population, which had swollen because of refugees moving into the town, how were they going to be secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And then the following day it just -- it stepped up and stepped up until -- and the attack started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So when you stay it stepped up and stepped up until the attack started, who started an attack, and when was this? How many days after this -- this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The attack was -- there was fighting at a low level going on all the time, exchanges of gunfire, exchanges of rocket -- RPG fire and things like that. What really signalled the start of it was the artillery fire, artillery and heavy mortar fire that suddenly started being fired by the HVO, and a general increase in the firing of -- of other weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when did this happen, after the meeting, and because you -- can you give an indication in time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I recall, it started properly the following day. I don't recall exactly when it started, but it would probably have been in the early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you a series of documents that relate to this particular meeting you've just been talking about, and I would first like you to look at Exhibit 1163. Just on the front page, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Again this is a Cheshire Regiment military info summary from the 16th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you move to page 3, and I'll read it out. Is it correct that in the last paragraph you -- of -- of this report, the text of the ultimatum as it's been read out is reported in this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, this is how it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who recorded this -- this particular text in this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This particular text is -- I -- I wrote it down in English following a translation from one of our translators that was in the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question on the text of this -- of this ultimatum. Let me read out the last sentence on page 3, which is the following: "The Bosnian media is to report the following in its bulletin: A list of the months that it should be reported that the HVO shelled no one and did not burn any houses and that all these actions were carried out by the Muslims." Now, was this actually the situation on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. The exact reverse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, after the -- after the text of the ultimatum there's -- there's a comment, and maybe you could read out that comment.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The comment says: "The BiH," that refers to the armija, "have stated that they cannot agree to all the demands. The HVO do not appear to be willing to negotiate their demands. Therefore an escalation of the conflict seems inevitable."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, that was a conclusion that was drawn by -- by UNPROFOR at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was drawn by everybody who was present in the room, the armija, the HVO, and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just move to another document, which is Exhibit 1162. Witness, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was shown it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just looking at the last page, who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Again Colonel Siljeg from OP zone North-west Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And to whom is the document addressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To the main staff of the HVO Croatian defence council in Mostar and to his own headquarters in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I refer you to the last paragraph on the second page.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would the text -- and we don't have to read it out, but what has been written there, would this have been in reference to the meeting you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if you just go to the last page of the document. Could you read out what's -- what's been recorded there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It says: "General Praljak sent them a message that they will be annihilated if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ BH."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who General Praljak was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We could then move to Exhibit 1182, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to the exhibit, would you look at page 2 of the document, please, and it refers to the Kralj Tomislav Brigade and then the Rama Brigade, and I note that tanks were mentioned. Now, you yourself, did you see any tanks in the locality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It refers here to the Kralj Tomislav Brigade. They're from Tomislavgrad as it states there. And the next brigade down, the Rama brigade is the Prozor brigade. The T-55 battle tank that they refer to in the third line that moved from Mount Makljen to Mount Crni Vrh or however you pronounce it. Mount Makljen is the Makljen checkpoint I indicated earlier on which is down here. The actual T-55 tank, like most soldiers who have tanks, they give each tank a name, and this particular tank was called Tvigi, and we knew it quite well. And as a result of the names they used to give their vehicles, we used to be able to track them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question on this. Did only the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Just a minute. [Interpretation] You said that the tank's name was Twiggy. Did you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- it was Tvigi, Your Honour, T-v-i-g-i. It was painted on the side of the turret in white letters about eight or nine inches high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This tank was well known in the region was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was by us, Your Honour. As you came off the Makljen checkpoint and around the bend in the road going down towards Prozor, you used to be able to see down into the main headquarters of the HVO there and you would regularly see the tank either there or up on the Makljen checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did the HVO have any more tanks between Tvigi?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was an M-48 old American tank that they had on the hill above Prozor. We never actually saw that tank move, and we were led to believe that when we saw it in different locations it was actually towed there, and it didn't actually work. The engine in it didn't actually work but the gun still did. And you used to see other armoured fighting vehicles. They had a BRDM 2 which is a type of four-wheeled armoured reconnaissance vehicle, Soviet, and the name of that one was James Dean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did the armija have tanks in the region?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In our region they didn't have tanks. As far as I'm aware, the nearest tank they had was a T-34 on the outskirts of Zenica, a T-34 being a Soviet World War II tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you take a look at Exhibit 1182, please. Again, top page. What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Again it's a Cheshire Regiment military information summary for the 17th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I could move your particular attention to the second page. The second part of -- of the first paragraph. And you don't have to -- well, just read it for yourself, but would this be the reaction of the Muslims to -- to the ultimatum as -- as it was issued and as you have been describing before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- this is from a debrief of the -- the Muslim officers who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So it says here that -- that he had been instructed from President Izetbegovic to reject the ultimatum. And this is a report dated the 17th of January. And so does that mean that -- yeah. Does that mean that -- I suppose that means that Izetbegovic has been informed about -- about this ultimatum directly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We -- within the base itself at Gornji Vakuf, in the office that I used, we had an INMARSAT, which is a satellite telephone. Whenever the people present at the negotiations in Gornji Vakuf needed to clarify or get permission for things, they used to use the INMARSAT and its associated facts to contact their relevant people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the third paragraph, which is the comment, and maybe you can read out this comment to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It says: "The situation in Gornji Vakuf appears to be deteriorating even further with the BiH," that's the armija, "rejection of the HVO demands. It is believed the HVO will try and enforce their demands soon after the deadline which is midnight. The likelihood of some elements of the BiH forces in the Bugojno area moving in to reinforce the BiH in Gornji Vakuf is looking greater. This would demonstrate a considerable escalation of the Muslim-Croat conflict effectively cutting the MSR." The MSR is an abbreviation for main supply route, which is what we called the route, because it was not only the aid convoys but it was our main supply route as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would this be the road that you've been marking on the map earlier as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, the MSR into Central Bosnia is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe we can look again at the ELMO or the -- yeah. It's -- yeah. If you could just point at -- at the road which is being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The MSR stretched from Vitez or what we referred to as the MSR stretched from Vitez down through Gornji Vakuf, onwards down through Prozor through Tomislavgrad and back to our rear base in Split. The cutting of the MSR would not only stop the aid convoys getting through, but it basically cut the supply line for our main force that was in Central Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now -- so the assessment made by UNPROFOR on the 17th of January was that there was a considerable escalation was -- was the likely result of -- of this meeting. Did this in fact happen as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one more document on -- on this particular ultimatum, which is Exhibit 1207. And maybe just before we break I'll just show this last document. What kind of document is this, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is a BBC press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you just explain, what was the position of UNPROFOR BritBat relating as far as media was concerned and especially international media?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Our command -- our overall commanding officer, Colonel Stewart, had a policy that the press could go where they liked and speak to who they wanted to, and if they couldn't get to where they wanted to get to, then we would take them in armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I point your attention to the second page, and could you please read out the second line on the -- on the -- the last but one paragraph starting with "HVO representative openly threatened"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what the foundation is for having a witness read from a press report. Perhaps Mr. Bos could clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, what I would like to know from this witness is whether what's been reported here, whether he would agree with the assessments that has been made here by the statement of the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So could you please read out that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Which paragraph again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The one but last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: From.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: With a deadline of 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "A deadline of 24 hours which expires on Sunday, i.e., midnight today was given for these demands which have been approved by the government of the so-called Herceg-Bosna to be fulfilled. Failing this, the HVO leaders have been warned, that they will not be responsible for the possible consequences. HVO representatives openly threatened that they were ready to use all available military might for the realisation of the demands of the ultimatum. The ultimatum which the HVO delivered to the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in Gornji Vakuf last night, the statement of the command of the 3rd Corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army says, is only a final example of a well planned and carefully prepared plan which has been realised in the Gornji Vakuf municipality since the 8th of January."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Would you agree with the assessment that has been made here by the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is the assessment of the UNPROFOR, yes. In that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Maybe it's a good time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one point of clarification, Mr. President, and that is was the BBC present at the meeting? Is this what the BBC was told by the BritBats UNPROFOR, and they're just regurgitating it here, or was it based on some independent evaluation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. To my knowledge the BBC were not present at the meeting. We did have a never ending stream of reporters from all news agencies moving back and through Gornji Vakuf and when this particular incident was going on marooned there and staying at our base. However, they would have been given -- we had a press officer in Vitez who would have briefed the press from -- the press had a house there that they shared with other agent -- other press agencies, the BBC, Associated Press and all those sorts of people, and they were briefed by a proper press officer from BritBat every day on any events and any questions that they had. So they would have been briefed on this ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's interesting, but I see that the -- the document itself describes the source of it as being radio Bosnia-Herzegovina Sarajevo, so it doesn't seem to tally with the witness's recollection of the thing. Perhaps Mr. Bos could clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, as you can see on the document, the source from the BBC seems to be Radio Sarajevo, which would have broadcast a programme on the -- at 1400 hours. What is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- if -- if the BBC say that that was their source, then for this particular press release then that is almost certainly the source that they're going to name, but in addition the representatives of all the press would also have been briefed by the press officer up in -- up in Vitez. At this stage, this particular attack was being shown on international TV all around the world. It was on -- we used to sit in the UN base watching ourselves on Sky TV. Whichever source that they've named for the press release, be it Radio Sarajevo or wherever, they would also have been briefed by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mention Sky channel, is this Sky News that was reporting live on the offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sky News reported several times during this -- this particular period. Their reporter on the spot was a gentleman, as I recall called Aernout van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see this on breaking news? Did you see this live? Did you see this programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used to watch Sky News all the time because it seemed a good source of news for us as well. In addition, Kate Adie, the esteemed BBC reporter used to come up there as well and film things -- and in fact got herself trapped in a building in Gornji Vakuf in the middle of a firefight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I to understand that the British army was informed directly by Sky News?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One point of clarification, Your Honour, on that same document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One point of clarification on that same document on paragraph 2, it says: "The HVO also demands that all members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army leave the town and proposes that joint military police patrols should be the only army military formations in Gornji Vakuf." Perhaps, you know, and if I were to read this the way I'm reading it, it would appear that nobody's supposed to be if Gornji Vakuf, neither army nor HVO, but you could have the presence of a joint military police. I wonder if the gentleman could expand on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was -- that was a proposal in the -- that they suggested, but the reality is that that's unworkable. Where would the HVO soldiers who came from Gornji Vakuf and whose families lived in Gornji Vakuf -- what about the armija soldiers who lived in Gornji Vakuf and whose families were in Gornji Vakuf? It was an unworkable proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now time to have a break, and we shall resume in 20 minutes. I should just like to tell the Prosecution that they've had an hour and a half so far. After that, we will have one hour left. If you could finish off your examination-in-chief today, that would be very good news.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Doubtful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to discuss with you the various HVO troops and units that you observed in the region during the conflict in January, February, 1993, and maybe we can do it in groups. Let me ask you first and some of this we've been referring to before but first to do it step-by-step. Which local HVO units were in Gornji Vakuf, could you say that, please, again?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was the Ante Starcevic brigade was the Gornji Vakuf HVO brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who commanded this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Zrinko Tokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were there any other HVO units or elements in the region?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was an element of the Bruno Busic Brigade who were called the Alfa Force and early on in our tour there was also a small HOS detachment, which is another type of Bosnian Croat militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How big was this HOS detachment? Do you know how many soldiers this involved?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was only a small group. It was probably -- no more than 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what HVO units outside the municipality of Gornji Vakuf were involved or did become involved in the conflict in January?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The next biggest one was the Ramska Brigade, the HVO from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who commanded this brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure of exactly who commanded it in the field but one of the senior commanders was a gentleman by the name of Petar Kolakusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You may have to spell this name for the court reporter, because -- could you please spell the name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I recall his name was spelled Kolakusic with an upside down roof on the C.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And his first name was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. So we've spoken about the Ramska Brigade. Any other brigades?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Tomislav brigade. The brigade next door to them from Livno. There were -- not the whole brigade, just elements from it. And there were other elements from other brigades all across Herzegovina. There were some troops there from Siroki Brijeg, Posusje, Grude, all over the place. Not as a complete tactical formation, just probably as reinforcements to reinforce the brigades that were going to carry out the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've mentioned the Tomislav brigade. Do you know who commanded this brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was commanded by a Canadian gentleman called Nick Glasnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you take a look at Exhibit 1107. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was shown it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Colonel Siljeg, the commander of OP zone North-west Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And to is this order addressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To all OP zones. I'm not quite sure what S/Z means. I assume it means all subordinate brigades to that OP zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And which OP zone are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: North-west Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What's the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 12th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you read the first paragraph of this order it makes reference to an incident on a Croatian flag taken down in the centre of town. Is this the same incident that you've been talking about before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And it also talks about the arrival of BH army forces from Central Bosnia in Gornji Vakuf. Do you know what this order is referring to here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This refers to the Jajce brigade or Jajce brigade - however you pronounce it - the armija brigade that moved into that area, or the remnants of it after the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you tell us again how many soldiers were involved in the -- in this brigade. How many soldiers of this brigade actually moved into Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Into the town itself, as far as I'm aware, none moved into the town itself. They were billeted in villages on the edge of the town, and there were approximately 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, when you were shown this document yesterday, and you can glance through the document again, what kind of order -- how would you -- I don't know how to say that. How would you -- how would you describe this type of order? What kind of order is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This in military terminology is, in the British army, is what we would call a confirmatory order. There would have been a bigger set of orders for the commanders prior to this where they would have been given their tasks briefed on -- shown maps and discussed all through properly. And then provided there were no major changes to the commander's intent, he would then have issued a confirmatory order confirming it and this would appear to be a confirmatory order confirming an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What would be the time spent between these more detailed orders and a confirmatory order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I'm going to object. It calls for speculation. First of all, while he's reading it and he tell us what he believes it is, he hasn't made a foundation to tell us whether he actually knows if there are any other previous meetings or orders for this particular order. So if he could give us step-by-step that's the first step.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most armies --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object again. He can tell us specifically as to the HVO. What the British army does is different. Unless he's going to tell us that the British army is trained in the same fashion as the HVO was or vice versa I should say, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can read this order. On reading this order, do you think it tallies with the way the HVO operated and the way you perceived things on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the confirmatory order for a deliberate attack on Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bos, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, glancing through this document again, would the units that are being referred to in this document, would you have seen these units operating in Gornji Vakuf at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At item 3.4, two tanks are mentioned it seems. On page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were more tanks for the assault on Gornji Vakuf than just the single tank that came, the T-55 that I mentioned earlier, Tvigi, from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did the other tank come from if Tvigi was there? If there's Tvigi and no James Dean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other two tanks according to these orders came from the Tomislav brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just looking at this order and -- who would be the overall commander of the troops that are referred to in this record?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The field commander would be Colonel Siljeg himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, we've spoke briefly today about some brigades that were commanded directly from Mostar. Could you repeat again the names of these -- these brigades?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade and the Bruno Busic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how would you label these type of brigades? How would you describe them? What was their function in the field?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade was -- appeared to be a commander's reserve, an operational manoeuvre group. The Bruno Busic Brigade appeared to be a brigade of troops that did things like long-range reconnaissance and similar sort of stuff like that. Bruno Busic Brigade was based in small units in -- in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade was an operational manoeuvre group. Can you explain to the Judges what that means?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is a complete unit that can be quickly deployed into an area to either reinforce an attack, reinforce a defence or exploit an advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What can you say about the soldiers serving -- serving in these two brigades?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How can you compare them to regular HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were better equipped and seemed better organised. They were more soldierly than the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you look at Exhibit 1663, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, can you say that one again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. 1663. What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is again a military information summary from the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what's the date?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 14th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could I refer you first to page 2 under paragraph 5, and it makes reference here to a debrief of a British mercenary who was currently serving in the Bruno Busic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf and then it says information received on this debrief is attached to the annex in Annex A of this report. So if you go to the next page, would that be the Annex A to the report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were you the person who actually debriefed this British mercenary?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, just a question on what's been written down here in this annex. As far as paragraph 4 is concerned, it says: "The international are trained in Croatia and are funded and paid by Croatia itself." Was the person that you debriefed also a person who was trained in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He initially was a former British soldier like it said. He'd also fault as a mercenary for the Croatian army in Osijek, and when Croatia was stable, the -- he and the mercenaries that were with him were then seconded to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And now if you could please move to Exhibit 8572.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. This British mercenary whom you debriefed, this person had a two-year contract. Who had he signed this contract with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the Croatian army, Your Honour. The Croatian Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Karnavas. How was he paid, in a bank account in Switzerland, in cash? How was he paid, in German marks, in dinars? Did you discuss this with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As it says in the report, he was paid into a bank account in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he tell you which bank this money was paid into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just Zagreb, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After your debrief, what happened to this mercenary? Did he go back to the UK, or did he stay on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mercenary, we cultured a relationship with the mercenary because he was British and he was a former part-time British soldier. He used to be quite chatty with us, and we used to bring him into the base and let him watch British television and allow him to use our mail facilities so that he could write to people back in the UK. The last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were watching Sky News.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Amongst other things, Your Honour, yes. The last time I'd heard of him he had been arrested back in the UK by Special Branch about three or four years after this for whatever reason. Special Branch probably arrested him because of his mercenary connections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. When he was part of this unit, how did he cope? Did he speak B/C/S? How did he communicate with his fellow men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He spoke Serbo-Croat, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to point out here it says here in item number 1 that the reliability of this information cannot be assessed, and so I just want to point that out for the record. I think that's something that perhaps the gentleman can tell us what does he mean by that since it cannot be assessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, why -- I think these are questions that should be raised in cross-examination. I don't understand why these questions need to be answered now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that can be raised at a later stage, but perhaps the Defence won't go back to it. Now, you said reliability -- it says reliability cannot be assessed. Why did you put that down? Did you doubt what he said? Why did you see fit to make that note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the first time I'd spoken to him, Your Honour and we had nothing to compare with what he said to other people. We graded sources from A to F, 1 to 6. An F6 source would be -- at that stage you would not be able to grade the information or compare it because you had nothing to compare it with. But as I said, we developed a relationship with him over a period of time. I also said that we used to allow him to use our mail facilities because there was no post in Central Bosnia. That was part of how we verified a lot of what he said in that he was writing to -- back to the UK to mercenary recruiters commenting on the quality of other mercenaries that he was with and could they get any more and such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to the admission of this exhibit for two reasons. One, it was compiled in mid-March, 1993, and the indictment with respect to Gornji Vakuf, and the witness is speaking about Gornji Vakuf towards the end of 1992 and January, 1993. So I don't think that this document is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll make note of that. Mr. Bos, the Judges will deliberate. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If you look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Bos, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you look at Exhibit 8572, please. What does this document depict?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is the armed flash of the Alpha force of the Bruno Busic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you the one who drew this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I drew it and that's my signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any military police units involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. You're moving on to something else. Now, the drawing there, is that the badge, the flash that he had on him when you debriefed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At that time we used to buy, if we could, the badges off them and send them back up the chain of command, so you start compiling a library of unit insignia. I actually bought his badge off him for 10 marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You paid 10 marks for this flash, and you have it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour. It's then passed up the chain of command and it was used to compile a library of different units' insignias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that between Alpha Force there's a square and a chequer-board under the bird's feet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the Croatian red and white chequer-board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Witness, we're -- the question I had put to you in -- just some time earlier was were there any military police units involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know where these military units -- police units came from?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how would you recognise these military police units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They tended to wear blue helmets, and they tended to use blue-painted vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know what their role was in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Their role was -- appeared to be rear security in that they were securing the areas behind the front line, behind the Muslim-Croat front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you look at Exhibit 1053, please. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was shown it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's the 5th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, you say 1993, but does that actually --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, the 5th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What is said after the 5th of January? Which number is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a 3. Who signed this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Somebody called Valentin Coric or Coric or Korik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: To whom is the report addressed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's addressed personally to Bruno Stojic, the head of the department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Does this document talk about the involvement of military police units in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document that you have before you, what was the mission assigned to the military police? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is -- its rear security duties, Your Honour, protecting the population, populated areas, restoring road traffic, diffusing fear among the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which begs the question, would that have been necessary? If he's going to be raising these sort of documents, the gentleman was there at the time. Perhaps he can tell us, was this necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Was it really necessary to specify that the military police had as their principal objective to protect the population in populated areas, restore road traffic and so on? Was it necessary to remind them of their duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
