utterances.text: The document is a situation report, and it's the commander of the military police explaining the situation to the head of the Department of Defence what they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But my question, Your Honour, and the gentlemen hasn't answered it, was since he was there, based on what was happening at the time, because I understand he has indicated that there was sporadic activity, was this necessary activity at that -- at that point and place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it really necessary for the military police to deploy in the territory in view of the activity? Because this is a 5th of January document. I just noted that the date there was the 5th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The deployment of military police would have been required. It would be primarily, like it says in the document, to maintain order, but it would be also implying that they were to -- to do -- to carry out these missions, they would have to stop the reinforcement of Gornji Vakuf by outside armija units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you yourself -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I really would like to raise the following questions that in that interim report, the last paragraph of it in the English translation, we can read that. "The basic purpose of this operation is to preserve law and order, protect the population and populated areas, restore road traffic and defuse fear among the Croatian population in the said municipalities." Now, my question is if, according to our own recollections, since you have been there in the field, if you have -- you may be able to confirm that it has been done by the police or have you seen military police, I mean, or have you seen any other kind of activities which they carried out? Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They established checkpoints on the roads and reinforced checkpoints that were already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, sir. Being there, can you tell us something about the security situation? Was there unrest? Were there many crimes? Was there a situation where people didn't dare to go out, which called for a special police protection of order and security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As -- as you can see from the map, Your Honour, the -- the population is fairly intermingled ethnic-wise. As for the level of crime, that I can't comment on, but there would obviously be a fear that the other side would do something unless they protected themselves. The military police, by their presence, would allay the local Croat fears, local Croats in the villages fears of being attacked by the armija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You yourself, did you see any military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And in military terms, did you gain the impression that belonged to -- that they belong to a well-structured, disciplined unit, loyal, following orders, confronting problems? What was the impression that they left on you this military police unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- I couldn't tell -- I couldn't tell you specifically of the military police that I encountered which ones came from which unit. However, the ones that I did encounter were mainly manning roadblocks. There's not a lot you can say about what they were doing on the roadblocks other than they were stopping vehicles, but they seemed to be just manning the roadblocks and controlling traffic at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There's another question from the Bench. Military police is always an interesting subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, staying with that same paragraph on the military police objectives, why does it only mention the Croatian population and not the population in general? Can you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't expand on it properly, but I can pass comment on it in that the -- the HVO military police would be more concerned with the security of Croatian areas than they would be with the security of Muslim areas. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We're not receiving the interpretation. No interpretation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a technical problem. Is that all right now? Yes? So what you're saying is that the military police was preoccupied with the Croats because this was Croat territory predominantly; is that right? Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- the military police of the HVO would be more concerned with the security of the Croatian community than with the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was there also a military police of the ABiH which protected the Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- there were some military police of -- in the armija but not that many. Village defence tended to revolve around the TO, which is like a sort of armija militia. A lot of Muslim villages had weapons in them and semi-trained people in the village, residents, if you will, who would provide the local security for the village. Villages of tactical importance at specific phases would then have proper armija troops in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to show you two other documents relating to the military police, and if you just would first go to Exhibit 1635, please. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's the same person that wrote the previous document, Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And to whom is it addressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's to Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The 9th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Putting your attention to the second paragraph of this -- this order and in particular the last sentence. Does this report talk about and in particular this last sentence about military police particularly in the region of Prozor and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's -- sorry. The second paragraph on page 1.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then all the way at the bottom, the last sentence. Maybe you can read out that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "One military battalion is active in each of the operational zones and the 1st Light Assault Battalion is active in the entire territory of HZ HB," which is Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This is -- no, you're now reading out the second line, but I was asking you to read out the last line of this paragraph -- of this second paragraph, starting with the word "Around." It's -- I'll read it out to you, Witness. "Around 100 military policeman participated in Prozor and 370 in Gornji Vakuf and Central Bosnia. The active service company of the 4th military police battalion." Now, were these numbers -- were these numbers mean -- would they be reasonable in how you -- what you saw on the ground as far as military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to trespass again on matters on which Your Honours have already ruled, but it seems to me that Mr. Bos's testimony would be just as useful as the witness's on that point. It's just absolute sheer speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this witness said he saw military police on the ground. My question is, reading these numbers, would that be a reasonable number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how the question should have been asked: You were in the field. Did you see the military police in combat action? Not patrolling the roads or providing security, but taking part in combat? Because the document that we see here, it would appear that in Gornji Vakuf the military police took part in the fighting and that they had eight dead and 64 wounded. Now, did you have any knowledge of that, of military police killed in combat? And the numbers there are significant for killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware that the military police were in the Gornji Vakuf area, Your Honour. The actual amount of military police I couldn't verify, but there were a lot of them. I personally did not see them fighting. However, I spoke to people who did see them fighting, and I was also present and on the outside of negotiations between the two sides in which their actions were brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one can conclude that according to you they did participate in combat. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And there was one particular incident that occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Prosecutor Bos is going to bring it up in a bit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you know in advance the questions that you're going to be asked. Mr. Bos, go on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Refer to what you were going to say?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A specific incident where the military police cleansed a village called Hrasnica, which is just to the north of Gornji Vakuf -- slightly to the east of the main road running from Gornji Vakuf to Bugojno. This village was attacked three times. Each attack was worse than the one previously. Eventually the village was totally destroyed. The -- this particular action was brought up during cease-fire negotiations, and there was no denial by the HVO that it was their forces had done it and there was no denial that it was the MPs that had done it. Witness reports from that particular attack identified one MP armoured vehicle, military police armoured vehicle, and also two military police troop carriers as being part of that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I may ask you a few more detailed questions about that later on, but just to finish off the involvement of military police unit, I would like you to look at one more document, which is Exhibit 3090. Looking at the front page of -- let me first ask you, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think it was a document I saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just reading from the front page, what is the title of the document? What kind of report is this? Maybe you could read it out.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is a report on the work of the HZ HB, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna military police, and the analysis of the situation for the period January to June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And whose name is underneath there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The same as the previous documents, Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, not to waste any time, let me please direct your attention -- attention to -- to page 6 of this report. And I'm particularly interested in the last three paragraphs on this page. Is it correct that it talks about here about an overall attack launched by HVO units and HVO military units on the 18th of January at 4.00?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On villages in dominating hill positions in the area held by the ABiH units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could you maybe please, just for the record, read out the last paragraph of this report on this page.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "About 0800 hours on the same day the military police 2nd Battalion members from Livno and Posusje, consisted of 30 military policemen, have taken control over the village of Uzricje by which the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina circle around the town was penetrated. At 1435 hours, the military police 1st Light Assault Battalion members took control over the village of Zdrince and most of the territory of this village was previously controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions on this paragraph. As referred to by the Judge earlier, would it be correct that this paragraph talks about the involvement of military police in military action?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And it talks about the village of Uzricje and it says, "by which the ABiH circle around the town was penetrated." Could you comment on that, please, what -- would you agree with this, with what has been said here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. At that period in time they -- what they would have been trying to achieve was like I mentioned earlier, rear security. To achieve that rear security, they would have had to take control of the Muslim villages to prevent the reinforcement of Gornji Vakuf and also to eliminate the possibility of involvement of fighters from those villages on their rear areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But does that mean that they would have had to penetrate an ABiH circle around the town?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. There would obviously have been some fortifications, maybe a couple of fire trenches and possibly a bunker, but not as it says, as it implies there. There it implies it was some sort of major defence, which was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever encounter HV troops in the Gornji Vakuf region in January -- well, during the time that you were serving in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can you tell us when that was and what -- what units you encountered?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I encountered the HVO field hospital in Rumboci which is just to the west of Prozor a colonel from a -- a surgeon colonel from the Croatian army. I asked him why he was there and he informed me that that area was part of Split military distinct. On another occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When was -- when did you encounter this -- this person at the hospital in Rumboci? Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not exactly, no. I'm afraid I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I actually met that gentleman twice. The -- on another occasion just outside the town of Bugojno, there was an HVO artillery position. On the way up there to -- to count the guns that they had and see what calibres they were, I encountered a small group of HV soldiers, Croatian army soldiers, from an air defence unit in Split, and on another occasion I encountered a platoon of Croatian army soldiers in the town of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Talking about the -- so are you now saying that there were two different occasions that you met these Croatian army soldiers from the air defence unit in Split?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. The air defence unit -- the air defence section from Split were near to the HVO gun line above the town of Bugojno, which is about here up. They were about here on the map, that being the town of Bugojno, and they were around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've just been pointing at the map again on the ELMO. Maybe you can put a mark where you actually encountered this.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would have to see a proper detailed map because the gun line was on a ridge line overlooking the town of Bugojno, but it would have probably been somewhere in that area there. That was a small section of Croatian army. They had an arm flash on their uniform of two crossed SA-7 missile launches.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was the presence of HV units in the area ever brought up in meetings with senior officials in which you participated as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what would be the actual response to such kind of allegations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Non-committal. They would neither confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. It seems to be working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you look at Exhibit 169 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before we move on to another document, in the last document could you go to page 7 of the English version. The penultimate paragraph. It is mentioned that in the month of January there were 430 military policemen engaged in Gornji Vakuf. 154 were members of the 1st Battalion. 243 members of the 2nd Battalion and 32 members of the 3rd Battalion. 430 military policemen all in all. Ten were wounded and 63 -- 10 were killed and 63 were wounded. Was it a surprise for you to see that hundreds of military policemen were engaged in battle? Does this mean that they were, so to speak, alone on the ground? And if that was not the case, there were the HVO units and the brigades you've just mentioned. So all in all, how many men were there on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the assault of Gornji Vakuf there were over two brigades, two reinforced brigades of soldiers on the ground. There were in excess of -- there were over 3.000 soldiers involved in it from the figures that we managed to get from the commanders at the time during the cease-fire negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In military terms, if you talk about 3.000 soldiers, is this a -- a large-scale offensive, a small-scale offensive, or medium-scale offensive? I mean in military terms. I don't know. I don't quite know what this kind of figure means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the context of the war in Bosnia, that is quite a large -- for an area of that size, that is quite a large offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In military terms, was it really necessary to have the military police there? They were well equipped. You said a while ago you talked about armoured vehicles. Was their presence really necessary, or was it necessary because they were perhaps better equipped or better armed? How can you explain this, such an offensive? Why were these people needed? And just as an example, if the British army were to launch an offensive of this kind, would they call upon the military police to come and give them a helping hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The actual point of -- of combat, Your Honour, would have been the town itself of Gornji Vakuf, and so the infantry and tanks and artillery and mortars of the HVO would have been directed at that. The military police would have been used to secure the rear areas, as I said earlier. However, I think that they grossly underestimated the ability of the villagers and the TO in the villages to fight, hence their quite high casualty rate. They only had a limited number of front-line combat troops which would have been like I said directed at the town of Gornji Vakuf. They would not have been able to weaken their front line against the Serbs to get more combat troops to do those sort of roles. And so the military police would have set up an outer cordon around the operation, which would necessitate securing the Muslim villagers so they couldn't interfere and securing the routes into and out of the main combat zone, which was the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we were talking about the involvement of HV units in the area, and I was about to show you an exhibit which is Exhibit 1698. Just looking at the front page again, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's the Cheshire Regiment military information summary from the 22nd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the third page, bottom paragraph. It refers to an encounter of 40 soldiers wearing 4th Brigade HV badges. Is this one of the encounters that you had described just earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I was actually present at that encounter. They were sat and gathered around a wall on the edge of the town with all their equipment, including sleeping bags, backpacks, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ask these soldiers why they were in the region?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They -- when I asked them why they were there through the interpreter, they said they were there for a wedding which I assumed to mean the wedding of Herceg-Bosna to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So interpreting your last comment, you did believe that they were there for wedding?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not a wedding wedding, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to restate my objection. The document is dated the end of March, 1993. The events that it addresses has nothing to do with the indictment and Gornji Vakuf that we're discussing. There is no indictment for that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the indictment, the presence of the HV is mentioned. Therefore, Witness, can you confirm having seen a unit belonging to the Croatian army with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the -- Your Honour, for the actual attack on the town of Gornji Vakuf, no, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In March, that was afterwards, you saw HV soldiers who were saying perhaps as if it were a joke that they were going to a wedding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to reach the spot where you saw them, did they have to pass HVO checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They were on the northern edge of the town of Prozor. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how were they equipped as far as you remember? Did they have armoured vehicles? What can you tell us about the way these soldiers were equipped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They didn't have armoured vehicles with them, but they had -- they were a platoon-sized group, and what caught our eye first of all was the fact that when you looked at them and when we saw them, we knew that they were not HVO. They were too well equipped. They were all young men. They were -- they had short hair. Their uniforms looked -- were all matching. They had ranks. They were wearing badges of ranks, and they had Austrian Sig-sauer assault rifles which were not standard issue for the HVO. And they had squad weapons as well. A squad weapon is a medium machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a platoon-sized group, Your Honour. Somewhere in the region of 30, 30 to 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, moving away from this -- from the topic of HV soldiers, I would like to ask you some questions about a person whose name has come up on a couple of occasions already, Zeljko Siljeg. Did you ever meet Zeljko Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I've met him. Not introduced to him, but I have met him numerous -- on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And on what occasions would you meet Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In cease-fire talks, moving him back and to cease-fire talks, in cigarette breaks during cease-fire talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you say moving him back and to cease-fire talks, were you in fact the one -- the person who was transporting Mr. Siljeg to cease-fire talks and back to his command post?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Whoever was available when it needed to be done would go and collect him, and I did it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What was Mr. Siljeg's position in the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was the colonel commanding OP zone North-west Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who would be the direct commander of Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It would be Brigadier Petkovic in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how would you describe the relationship between Siljeg, Mr. Siljeg and Petkovic as far as command control is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. First he's got lay a foundation. Let's just do it step-by-step. Has he observed it? On what basis can he make that -- draw that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll approach it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at Exhibit 1153, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object again on this. If this gentleman was not aware of this particular document at the time, then he's not capable of answering the question, you know, because he was asked -- if we go back to the original question. So in order for the gentleman to be able to give a precise answer as to command and control, first he must be asked whether he observed any interaction, not to be shown a document yesterday and then to come and say, "Ah, from here what can we see?" That's insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- were you ever attending meetings where Mr. Siljeg was also present?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I attended some of them where he was present, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And during those meetings, was there ever a reason for you to believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. He can ask what he observed in the meetings between General Petkovic and Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to be asking a totally different question. I did ask a question concerning local commanders so it didn't concern Mr. Siljeg directly but I shall ask the question again. When these high-level meetings were held, Colonel Siljeg was present. You were there sometimes also. So these were high-level meetings. When you attended they meetings, did the colonel give you the impression that he was controlling everything in military terms, or was he, as a military man -- did he have to refer to his superior? And if that was the case, who was his superior, and did he discuss this with you, or was he the person who was in control of everything in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the field commander for the attack, he was the controller for that. During cease-fire negotiations, he would occasionally ask for a recess so that he could go and get something cleared by somebody else, but who the somebody else was I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We are now going to address the core issue. He asked the meeting to be suspended. He left the room to go and make a telephone call, to go to talk to someone, to go and read the paper, and when he left the room, how long did his absence last? What did he say when he came back into the room? Do you remember any of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes he would just leave the room, and he would use a phone. Whether it was a satellite-type phone. Sometimes he would actually go back to his own headquarters and then come back with an answer. It varied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of answer did he come back with? He couldn't take the decision himself. Some higher authority had to vet this beforehand. If you remember, who could that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the -- the -- some of the stuff in the cease-fire agreements had to be vetted by a higher authority, and I assume because of the HVO command structure that that higher authority was Brigadier Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying because of the command structure of the HVO. Were you familiar with the command structure of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- by asking commanders which brigade they belonged to, which OP zone they belonged to and things like that during patrols and during meetings and what not, we had a -- what we call a family tree, and Colonel Siljeg was the head of OP zone North-west Herzegovina, and his superior was the commander of the HVO, which is Brigadier Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in your milinfosums, did you describe the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The -- if you flick through these documents, you will find several pages and several reports of where we say the commander of this is so-and-so and he's subordinate to him, and the commander of this unit is such-and-such a person, and his second in command is such-and-such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the clock. It's 7.00. I don't know, this is probably a good time to break. I'm not finished yet, and I think I'll take -- I have to take at least -- well, I think I need another 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume tomorrow. If the Defence teams cannot finish tomorrow, the witness will have to stay on until Wednesday but much will depend on the questions that will be asked. It's now 7.00, and I invite you to come back tomorrow afternoon because the hearings will be in the afternoon this week. We shall resume at a quarter past 2.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
